en: Parivāra 11.
Adhikaraṇabheda 1. Ukkoṭanabhedādi (The Division of Legal Matters: Opening Again, etc.)
There are four kinds of legal issues:
the legal issue arising from a dispute, the legal issue arising from an accusation, the legal issue arising from an offense, and the legal issue arising from business—
these are the four kinds of legal issues.
How many reopenings are there for these four kinds of legal issues?
There are ten reopenings for these four kinds of legal issues:

two reopenings for a legal issue arising from a dispute, four reopenings for a legal issue arising from an accusation, three reopenings for a legal issue arising from an offense, and one reopening for a legal issue arising from business.
These are the ten reopenings of these four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
When reopening a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), how many methods of settling (*samatha*) does one reopen?
When reopening a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), how many methods of settling does one reopen?
When reopening a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), how many methods of settlement (*samatha*) does one reopen?
When reopening a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), how many methods of settlement does one reopen?
When reopening a legal issue concerning a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), one reopens two methods of settlement.
One who reopens a legal issue concerning an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) reopens four methods of settling disputes (samatha).
One who reopens a legal issue concerning an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) reopens three methods of settling disputes.
One who reopens a legal issue concerning business (kiccādhikaraṇa) reopens one method of settling disputes.
How many kinds of reopening are there?
In how many ways does the reopening of a legal issue arise?
Endowed with how many factors does a person reopen a legal issue?
How many persons incur an offense by reopening a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)?
There are twelve reopenings.
One brings about a reopening in ten ways.
A person endowed with four factors reopens a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
How many persons, while reopening a legal issue, incur an offense?
What are the twelve reopenings (*ukkoṭa*)?
An act not performed; an ill-performed act; an act to be performed again; one not settled; one poorly settled; one to be settled again;
one not adjudicated; one poorly adjudicated; one to be adjudicated again; one not pacified; one poorly pacified;
and one to be pacified again.
These are the twelve reopenings.
By what ten modes does one bring about a reopening?
Therein, one reopens a legal issue that has arisen; there, one reopens a legal issue that has arisen and been settled.
He reopens a legal issue on the way; he reopens a legal issue that has been settled on the way;
he reopens a legal issue once it has reached that place; he reopens a legal issue that has been settled once it has reached that place; he reopens a resolution through recollection;
he reopens a resolution because of past insanity; he reopens a verdict of further penalty; he reopens a covering over as with grass.
In these ten ways, one brings about the reopening of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
Endowed with which four factors does a person reopen a legal issue?

One reopens a legal issue by falling into a state of partiality through desire; one reopens a legal issue by falling into a state of partiality through hatred; one reopens a legal issue by falling into a state of partiality through delusion; one reopens a legal issue by falling into a state of partiality through fear.
A person endowed with these four factors reopens a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
Which four persons, while reopening a legal issue, incur an offense? One who has been ordained that very day reopens it:

an offense of expiation for reopening; a newcomer reopens it: an offense of expiation for reopening; one who acts as an agent reopens it: an offense of expiation for reopening; one who gives consent reopens it: an offense of expiation for reopening.
These four persons incur an offense by reopening a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
2. The Source of the Legal Issue, etc.:
What is the source of a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, and what is its origination?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the legal issue concerning accusations?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the legal issue concerning offenses?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the legal issue concerning duties?
The legal issue of dispute has dispute as its source, its origin, its birth, its provenance, its equipment, and its origination.
The legal issue of accusation has accusation as its source, its origin, its birth, its provenance, its equipment, and its origination.
The legal issue of offense has offense as its source, its origin, its birth, its provenance, its equipment, and its origination.
A legal issue arising from business has business as its source, business as its origin, business as its birth, business as its provenance, business as its equipment, and business as its origination.
What is the source of a legal issue arising from dispute? What is its origin, what its birth, what its provenance, what its equipment, what its origination?
A legal issue arising from censure … [and so on] …

What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the legal issue concerning offenses …pe… the legal issue concerning business?
The legal issue concerning disputes has cause as its source, cause as its origin, cause as its birth, cause as its provenance, cause as its equipment, and cause as its origination.

The legal issue of reproach …pe… the legal issue of an offense …pe… the legal issue of business has its cause as its source, its cause as its origin, its cause as its birth, its cause as its arising, its cause as its equipment, and its cause as its manifestation.
What is the source of a legal issue arising from a dispute? What is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, and what is its origination?
[The same applies to] a legal issue arising from an accusation …pe… a legal issue arising from an offense …pe…
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)?

A legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) has conditions as its source, conditions as its origin, conditions as its birth, conditions as its provenance, conditions as its equipment, and conditions as its origination.
A legal issue arising from censure (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*)... [and so on].

The legal issue concerning offenses …pe… the legal issue concerning business has its condition as its source, its condition as its origin, its condition as its birth, its condition as its provenance, its condition as its equipment, and its condition as its manifestation. 3.
The Roots of Legal Issues, etc.
Of the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), how many roots (*mūla*) are there, and how many origins (*samuṭṭhāna*)?
There are thirty-three roots and thirty-three origins for the four kinds of legal issues.
What are the thirty-three roots of the four kinds of legal issues?

There are twelve roots for a legal issue arising from a dispute, fourteen roots for a legal issue arising from an accusation, six roots for a legal issue arising from an offense, and one root for a legal issue arising from business—the Saṅgha itself.
These are the thirty-three roots of the four types of legal issues.
What are the thirty-three origins of the four types of legal issues?
The eighteen bases for schism are the origin of the legal issue arising from a dispute; the four failures are the origin of the legal issue arising from an accusation;
the seven classes of offenses are the origin of the legal issue arising from an offense; and the four formal acts are the origin of the legal issue arising from business.
These are the thirty-three origins of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
4. Regarding offenses conditioned by legal issues:
Is a legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) an offense or not an offense?
A legal issue arising from a dispute is not itself an offense.
But could one incur an offense by reason of a legal issue arising from a dispute?
Yes, one could incur an offense by reason of a legal issue arising from a dispute.
On account of a legal issue arising from a dispute, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a legal issue arising from a dispute, one incurs two offenses:
if one reviles one who is fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one reviles one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Due to this legal issue arising from a dispute, one incurs these two offenses.
To which of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which one is it?
Of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), by how many classes of offenses is it comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses (*āpattisamudāna*), from how many origins does it arise?
By how many legal issues, in how many places, and by how many means of settlement are they settled?
Those offenses belong to one of the four failures—
namely, failure in conduct.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is an issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven classes of offenses, it is included within two classes of offenses:
it may be a class of offenses involving an offense of expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of offenses involving an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from three origins.
From one legal issue:
the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
In three places—
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual—
it is settled by means of three methods of settling.

It may be by means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and acting according to what is admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*); it may be by means of resolution face-to-face and covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
Is a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) an offense (*āpatti*) or not? A legal issue arising from an accusation is not an offense.
But could one incur an offense on account of a legal issue arising from an accusation?
Yes, one could incur an offense on account of a legal issue arising from an accusation.
On account of a legal issue arising from an accusation, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of a legal issue arising from groundless accusation, one incurs three offenses:
if one accuses a bhikkhu with a groundless offense entailing expulsion (pārājika), it is an offense of formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa);
if one accuses him with a groundless offense of formal meeting of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one accuses another of a groundless failure in conduct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
On account of this legal issue arising from an accusation, one incurs these three offenses.
To which of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the four kinds of legal issues, which one is it?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses is it comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins does it originate?
By how many legal issues, in how many places, and by how many means of settlement are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is an issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven classes of offenses, it is included within three classes of offenses:

it may be a class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), it may be a class of offenses involving expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of offenses involving wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from three origins.
Those offenses which are grave originate from one legal issue:
the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
In one place—
in the midst of the Saṅgha—
it is settled by two means of settling.
By means of resolution face-to-face and by means of acting according to what has been admitted.
Those offenses which are light are [resolved] by one legal issue—
the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
In three places—
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual—
it is settled by means of three methods of settlement.
It may be settled both by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; it may be settled both by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
Is a legal issue arising from an offense an offense?
A legal issue arising from an offense is an offense.
But could one incur an offense by reason of a legal issue arising from an offense?
Yes, one could incur an offense by reason of a legal issue arising from an offense.
How many offenses does one incur by reason of a legal issue arising from an offense?
On account of a legal issue arising from an offense, one incurs four types of offenses:
if a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals an offense entailing defeat, she incurs an offense entailing defeat;
if she conceals it while being in doubt, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If a bhikkhu conceals a *saṅghādisesa* offense, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*);
if he conceals a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
On account of the legal issue arising from an offense, he incurs these four offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
To which of the four legal issues do they pertain?
By how many of the seven classes of offenses are they subsumed?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins do they originate?
By how many legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), in how many places, and by how many means of settlement (*samatha*) are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures (*vipatti*).
It may be a failure in virtue; it may be a failure in conduct.
Among the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven classes of offenses, it is included within four classes of offenses.

It may be a class of offense involving defeat (pārājika), it may be a class of grave offense (thullaccaya), it may be a class of offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), or it may be a class of offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from body, speech, and mind.
That offense which is an *anavaśeṣa* (inexhaustible) offense is not settled by any legal question (*adhikaraṇa*), nor in any place, nor by any means of settlement (*samatha*).
Those offenses which are light are [settled] by one legal question:
the legal question of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
In three places—
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual—
they are settled by means of three methods of settling.
It may be settled both by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; it may be settled both by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
Is a legal issue concerning business a transgression or not a transgression?
A legal issue concerning business is not a transgression.
But could one incur an offense conditioned by a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)?
Yes, one could incur an offense conditioned by a legal issue concerning business.
How many offenses does one incur conditioned by a legal issue concerning business?
On account of a legal issue arising from what ought to be done, one incurs five offenses:
when a nun who sides with one who has been suspended does not desist even after being exhorted up to the third time, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the motion;
and there are offenses of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*) at the two subsequent formal proclamations.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*);
if the monks who side with the schism do not desist after being formally admonished up to three times, there is an offense of communal transgression (*saṅghādisesa*);
if they do not desist from a wicked view after being formally admonished up to three times, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Due to a legal issue arising from what ought to be done, one incurs these five offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
To which of the four legal issues does it belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
By how many legal issues, in how many instances, and by how many means of settlement are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue or a failure in conduct.
Among the four types of legal issues, they are an issue concerning an offense.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within five classes of offenses:

they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), the class of grave offenses (thullaccaya), the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya), or the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from body, speech, and mind.
That offense which is *anavaśeṣa* (inexhaustible) is not settled by any legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), nor in any place, nor by any means of settlement (*samatha*).
That offense which is grave (*garuka*) is settled by one legal issue.
By means of a legal issue arising from duty;
in one place— that is,
in the midst of the Saṅgha.
It is settled by two methods of settling:
by resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
Those offenses which are light are [settled] by one legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
By means of a legal issue arising from duty;
in three places:
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual.
They are settled by three means of settling:
it may be by means of resolution face-to-face and acting according to what has been admitted; or it may be by means of resolution face-to-face and covering over as with grass.
5. The Intention Regarding Legal Issues.
There is a legal issue arising from a dispute that is also a legal issue arising from an accusation, a legal issue arising from an offense, and a legal issue arising from business.
There is a legal issue arising from a dispute that is not a legal issue arising from an accusation, nor a legal issue arising from an offense, nor a legal issue arising from business;

nevertheless, conditioned by a legal issue arising from a dispute, there arises a legal issue arising from an accusation, a legal issue arising from an offense, and a legal issue arising from business.
In what way, how so?
Here, monks dispute:
"This is Dhamma" or "This is non-Dhamma," and so forth...
Whether it be a grave offense or a non-grave offense:

whatever quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, disagreement, speaking otherwise, contentious speech, or wrangling occurs therein—this is called a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
When the Saṅgha disputes over a legal issue arising from a dispute, that is a legal issue arising from a dispute.
When one disputes, it is a legal issue arising from a dispute (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
When, while disputing, one incurs an offense, it is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
When the Saṅgha performs a formal act on account of that offense, it is a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

Thus, on account of a legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa), there arises a legal issue arising from an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa), there arises a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), and there arises a legal issue arising from business (kiccādhikaraṇa).
A legal issue arising from an accusation may be a legal issue arising from an offense, it may be a legal issue arising from business, or it may be a legal issue arising from a dispute.
A legal issue arising from an accusation may not be a legal issue arising from an offense, it may not be a legal issue arising from business, and it may not be a legal issue arising from a dispute.
Furthermore, on account of a legal issue concerning censure, there may be a legal issue concerning an offense, a legal issue concerning business, or a legal issue concerning a dispute.
How so? Here, monks censure a monk for failure in virtue, or failure in conduct, or failure in view, or failure in livelihood.
Whatever there is therein of reproach, reproaching, reviling, censuring, compliance, encouragement, and lending support—this is called a legal issue arising from reproach (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
When the Saṅgha disputes over a legal issue arising from reproach, it is a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
One who is disputing reproaches; this is a legal issue arising from reproach.
When one being accused incurs an offense, it is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
When the Saṅgha performs a formal act on account of that offense, it is a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

Thus, conditioned by a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), there arises a legal issue arising from an offense, a legal issue arising from business, and a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
There is an offense-dispute, there is a business-dispute, there is a dispute-dispute, and there is an accusation-dispute.

There is no offense-dispute, no business-dispute, no dispute-dispute, and no accusation-dispute; nevertheless, conditioned by an offense-dispute, there arises a business-dispute, a dispute-dispute, and an accusation-dispute.
In what way?

The five classes of offenses constitute a legal issue arising from an offense; the seven classes of offenses also constitute a legal issue arising from an offense. This is called a legal issue arising from an offense.
When the Saṅgha disputes regarding a legal issue arising from an offense, it is a legal issue arising from a dispute.
When one disputes, it is a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
When one reproaches another, they incur an offense; this is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
On account of that offense, the Saṅgha performs a formal act; this is a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

In this way, conditioned by a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), there is a legal issue concerning business (kiccādhikaraṇa), there is a legal issue concerning disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa), and there is a legal issue concerning accusations (anuvādādhikaraṇa).
A legal issue concerning business may be a legal issue concerning disputes, it may be a legal issue concerning accusations, or it may be a legal issue arising from an offense.
A legal issue concerning business may not be a legal issue concerning disputes, it may not be a legal issue concerning accusations, and it may not be a legal issue arising from an offense.

Moreover, on account of a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), there arises a legal issue concerning dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue concerning censure (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), and a legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).

How so? Whatever constitutes the business and duty of the Saṅgha—whether a formal act by way of announcement (*apalokanakamma*), a formal act by a motion (*ñattikamma*), a formal act with a motion as the second part (*ñattidutiyakamma*), or a formal act with a motion as the fourth part (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—this is called a legal issue concerning business.
In a legal issue concerning duties, the Saṅgha disputes; this is a legal issue of dispute.
While disputing, one makes an accusation; this is a legal issue of accusation.
While accusing, one commits an offense; this is a legal issue of offense.
The Saṅgha performs a formal act regarding that offense; this is a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

Thus, by reason of a legal issue arising from business, there arises a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), and a legal issue arising from offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
6. The Section on Questions.
Where there is resolution through mindfulness, is there there resolution face-to-face?
Where there is resolution face-to-face, is there there resolution through mindfulness?
Where there is resolution because of past insanity, is there there resolution face-to-face?
Where there is resolution face-to-face, is there there resolution because of past insanity?
Where there is acting according to what has been admitted, is there there resolution face-to-face?
Where there is resolution face-to-face, is there there acting according to what has been admitted?
Where there is a majority decision (yebhuyyasikā), is there there a resolution face-to-face (sammukhāvinaya)?
Where there is a resolution face-to-face, is there there a majority decision?
Where there is a verdict of further penalty (tassapāpiyasikā), is there there a resolution face-to-face?
Where there is resolution face-to-face, is there also adjudication for the worse?
Where there is covering over as with grass, is there also resolution face-to-face?
Where there is resolution face-to-face, is there also covering over as with grass?
7. Section on Resolution:

At whatever time a legal issue is settled by means of both resolution in the presence of the accused (*sammukhāvinaya*) and resolution through mindfulness (*sativinaya*)—wherever there is resolution through mindfulness, there is resolution in the presence;
wherever there is resolution in the presence, there is resolution through mindfulness.
In that case there is no decision on account of past insanity, nor is there acting according to what has been admitted, nor a majority decision,
nor a further penalty, nor covering over as with grass.
At whatever time [a dispute] is settled both by resolution face-to-face and by decision on account of past insanity …pe…

By means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by means of acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) … [and so on] … by means of resolution face-to-face and by means of majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) … [and so on] … by means of resolution face-to-face and by means of further penalty for a grave offense (*tassapāpiyasikā*) … [and so on] …
A legal issue is settled by means of resolution in the presence of the parties and by means of covering over as with grass.
Where there is covering over as with grass, there is resolution in the presence; where there is resolution in the presence, there is covering over as with grass.
Therein, there is no resolution through recollection, no resolution because of past insanity, no acting according to what has been admitted, and no...
Majority decision; there, the procedure for further penalty does not apply.
8. The Chapter on Association:
Are these two factors—namely, resolution face-to-face and resolution through recollection—associated or dissociated?
And is it possible, by repeatedly analyzing these matters, to point out their distinction?
[Is there] "settlement in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*) or "settlement for one no longer deluded" (*amūḷhavinaya*)? ...pe...
[Is there] "settlement in the presence" or "acting according to what is admitted" (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*)?
Whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *yebhuyyasikā*...
whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *tassapāpiyasikā*...
or whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *tiṇavatthāraka*—are these things associated (*saṃsaṭṭha*) or dissociated (*visaṃsaṭṭha*)?
And is it possible, having repeatedly analyzed these matters, to point out their distinction?
Whether it be "settlement in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*) or "settlement through recollection" (*sativinaya*)—
these matters are conjoined, not disjoined.
And it is not possible, having repeatedly separated these phenomena from one another, to point out a distinction between them:
whether as "settlement in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*) or "settlement for one no longer insane" (*amūḷhavinaya*) ...
[and so on] ... or as "settlement in the presence" or "acting according to what is admitted" (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
Either *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) or *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority);
or *sammukhāvinaya* or *tassapāpiyasikā* (reprimand for the worse);
or *sammukhāvinaya* or *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass).
These phenomena are conjoined, not disjoined;
and it is not possible, by repeatedly separating these phenomena one from another, to point out a difference between them.
9. The Source of the Seven Kinds of Serenity.
What is the source of *saṃmukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence), what is its origin, what is its nature, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, and what is its origination?
What is the source of *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection), what is its origin, what is its nature, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, and what is its origination?
What is the source of *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane), what is its origin, what is its nature, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, and what is its origination?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to admission)?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority)?
What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the *tassapāpiyasikā* (reprimand for greater wickedness)?
What is the source of the "covering over as with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka)? What is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance, what is its equipment, what is its origination?

The resolution face-to-face (sammukhāvinaya) is its source-source; it has the source as its origin, the source as its birth, the source as its provenance, the source as its equipment, and the source as its origination.
The resolution through mindfulness (sativinaya) ... [and so on] ...
The verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*)...

[as before] ...the verdict on admission (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) has its source in the origin, its source in the arising, its source in the birth, its source in the production, its source in the equipment, and its source in the origination.
The majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*)... [as before] ...

The *tassapāpiyasika* (decision for the worse) has its source in the cause, its origin in the cause, its birth from the cause, its production from the cause, its equipment in the cause, and its arising from the cause.

The *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) has its source in the cause, its origin in the cause, its birth from the cause, its production from the cause, its equipment in the cause, and its arising from the cause.
What is the source of *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence), what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its production, what is its equipment, and what is its arising?
Resolution through confession …pe… resolution for one who is no longer deluded …pe… acting according to what has been admitted …pe…

What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) …pe… of the further penalty (*tassapāpiyasikā*) …pe… and of the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*)?
Resolution face-to-face has its cause as its source, its cause as its origin, its cause as its birth, its cause as its arising, its cause as its equipment, and its cause as its manifestation.
So too for resolution through recollection...
resolution because of past insanity... [and so forth].
Acting according to what has been admitted has its source in a cause, its origin in a cause, its birth in a cause, its arising from a cause, its equipment in a cause, and its emergence from a cause.
A majority decision...

[and so on] ...a formal act of further penalty has its source in a cause, its origin in a cause, its birth in a cause, its arising from a cause, its equipment in a cause, and its emergence from a cause.
The "covering over as with grass" has a cause as its source, a cause as its origin, a cause as its birth, a cause as its arising, a cause as its equipment, and a cause as its manifestation.

What is the source of "resolution face-to-face"? What is its origin, its birth, its arising, its equipment, and its manifestation? [The same applies to] "resolution through recollection"... [and so forth].
...the verdict of past insanity ...pe...
acting according to what has been admitted ...pe...
the majority decision ...pe...

What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance, what is the equipment, and what is the origination of the verdict of past misdeeds (*tassapāpiyasikā*) … [and so on] … and of the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*)?

The verdict in the presence (*sammukhāvinaya*) has conditions as its source, conditions as its origin, conditions as its birth, conditions as its provenance, conditions as its equipment, and conditions as its origination.
Resolution through confession...
[and so on] ... resolution because of past insanity...

[and so on] ... acting according to what has been admitted has its condition as its source, its condition as its origin, its condition as its birth, its condition as its provenance, its condition as its equipment, and its condition as its manifestation.
The majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) ...

[and] the adjudication for further offense (*tassapāpiyasikā*) have their source in conditions, their origin in conditions, their birth from conditions, their arising from conditions, their equipment of conditions, and their manifestation from conditions.

The covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*) has its source in conditions, its origin in conditions, its birth from conditions, its arising from conditions, its equipment of conditions, and its manifestation from conditions.
How many roots and how many origins are there for the seven principles for settling disputes?
For the seven principles for settling disputes, there are twenty-six roots and thirty-six origins.
What are the twenty-six roots for the seven principles for settling disputes?
There are four roots for resolution face-to-face:
presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the person.
There are four roots for resolution through recollection.
There are four roots for resolution because of past insanity;
there are two roots for acting according to what has been admitted:
he who confesses and he to whom he confesses.
The four bases for a decision by majority;
the four bases for a formal act of further penalty;
the four bases for covering over as with grass.
Presence before the Saṅgha, presence before the Dhamma, presence before the Vinaya, and presence before the individuals—
these are the twenty-six roots of the seven principles for settling disputes.
What are the thirty-six origins of the seven principles for settling disputes?
The performance, the doing, the undertaking, the acceptance, the acquiescence, and the non-objection regarding the formal act of sativinaya;
[the same applies to] the formal act of amūḷhavinaya...
[and] the formal act of paṭiññātakaraṇa.

The performance, carrying out, acceptance, admission, endurance, and non-objection regarding a formal act by a majority vote, a formal act of further penalty, or a formal act of covering over as with grass.
These are the thirty-six origins of the seven methods of settling disputes (sattannaṃ samathānaṃ).
10. The Seven Methods of Settling Disputes:

Regarding the various meanings and expressions—whether it be "settlement in the presence" (sammukhāvinaya) or "settlement through recollection" (sativinaya)—are these things different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning with only the phrasing being different?
Whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *amūḷhavinaya* …pe… whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *paṭiññātakaraṇa* … whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *yebhuyyasikā*.
"Face-to-face settlement" (*sammukhāvinaya*) or "decision for the worse" (*tassapāpiyasikā*)...

or "face-to-face settlement" or "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*)—are these things different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning and only different in phrasing?
"Face-to-face settlement" or "settlement through recollection" (*sativinaya*)—these things are indeed different in meaning and different in phrasing.
Whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *amūḷhavinaya* …pe… whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *paṭiññātakaraṇa* … whether it be *sammukhāvinaya* or *yebhuyyasikā*.

"Settlement in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*) or "decision for the worse" (*tassapāpiyasikā*) … "settlement in the presence" or "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*): these things are different both in meaning and in phrasing.
Is dispute (*vivāda*) a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), or is dispute not a legal issue, or is it a legal issue but not a dispute, or is it both a legal issue and a dispute?

There may be a dispute that is a legal question arising from a dispute; there may be a dispute that is not a legal question; there may be a legal question that is not a dispute; and there may be that which is both a legal question and a dispute.
In this regard, what is a dispute that is a legal question arising from a dispute?
Here, monks dispute, saying either "it is Dhamma" or "it is non-Dhamma" … [and so on] …
Whether it be "an offense of a grave nature" or "an offense not of a grave nature"—
whatever quarrel, strife, contention, dispute, difference of opinion, speaking otherwise, contentious speech, or wrangling occurs therein—
this is a dispute that constitutes a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, what is a dispute that is not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)?
A mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother; a father disputes with his son, and a son disputes with his father;
a brother disputes with a brother, and a brother disputes with a sister; and a sister [disputes with a brother].
Brothers dispute, and companions also dispute with their companions—
this is a dispute that is not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is not a dispute?
The legal issue of reproval, the legal issue of an offense, and the legal issue of business—
this is a legal issue that is not a dispute.
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is also a dispute?
A legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is both a legal issue and a dispute.
Regarding censure (*anuvāda*): could it be a legal issue arising from censure; could it be censure that is not a legal issue; could it be a legal issue that is not censure;

and could it be both a legal issue and censure? It could be censure that is a legal issue arising from censure; it could be censure that is not a legal issue; it could be a legal issue that is not censure; and it could be both a legal issue and censure.
In this context, what is reproach as a legal issue arising from reproach?
Here, monks reproach a monk for failure in virtue, or failure in conduct, or failure in view, or failure in livelihood.
Whatever therein is reproaching, reproaching, alleging, speaking in accordance, compliance, encouragement, and lending support—that is [reproach].
This accusation is a legal issue arising from an accusation.
In this regard, what is an accusation that is not a legal issue?
A mother may accuse her son, a son may accuse his mother, a father may accuse his son, and a son may [accuse] his father.
The father speaks in conformity with [the son], the brother also speaks in conformity with the brother, the brother also speaks in conformity with the sister,
the sister also speaks in conformity with the brother, and the companion also speaks in conformity with the companion—
this is conformity, not a legal issue.
In this context, what is a legal issue that is not a formal accusation?
A legal issue concerning an offense, a legal issue concerning business, and a legal issue concerning a dispute—
this is a legal issue that is not a formal accusation.
In this regard, what is that which is both a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) and a formal accusation (*anuvāda*)?
A legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is both a legal issue and a formal accusation.

What is an offense (*āpatti*)? An offense is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). Is there an offense that is not a legal issue? Is there a legal issue that is not an offense? Is there that which is both a legal issue and an offense?

An offense may be a legal issue arising from an offense; it may be an offense that is not a legal issue; it may be a legal issue that is not an offense; or it may be both a legal issue and an offense.
In this regard, what is an offense that is a legal issue arising from an offense?
All five classes of offenses are legal issues arising from an offense.
The seven classes of offenses are a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
This offense is a legal issue arising from an offense.
In that regard, what is an offense that is not a legal issue?
The attainment of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-samāpatti*):
this is an offense (*āpatti*), not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
In that regard, what is a legal issue, not an offense?
A legal issue arising from business, a legal issue arising from dispute, and a legal issue arising from censure—
this is a legal issue that is not an offense.
In this context, what is a legal issue that is also an offense?
An offense-dispute (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is both a dispute and an offense.
Regarding what is a duty (*kicca*): Is it a duty-dispute (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), or is it a duty that is not a dispute, or is it a dispute that is not a duty, or is it both a dispute and a duty?
It may be a duty that is a duty-dispute; it may be a duty that is not a dispute; it may be a dispute that is not a duty; and it may be both a dispute and a duty.
In this context, what is a legal issue arising from business (kiccādhikaraṇa)?

Whatever constitutes the business or duty of the Saṅgha— namely, a formal act by way of notification (apalokanakamma), a formal act by a motion (ñattikamma), a formal act by a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), or a formal act by a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma)—
this is a legal issue arising from business.
In this context, what is a duty that is not a legal issue?
The duty toward a teacher, the duty toward a preceptor, the duty toward one who shares a preceptor, and the duty toward one who shares a teacher—
this is a duty that is not a legal issue.
In this context, what is a legal issue that is not a duty?
The legal issue of dispute, the legal issue of accusation, and the legal issue of offense—
this is a legal issue that is not a duty.
In this context, what is both a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) and a duty (*kicca*)?
It is the legal issue of duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), which is both a legal issue and a duty.
The classification of legal issues is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Legal issues, reopening,
formal modes, and persons.
By way of source, cause, and condition, by root, and by origin;
and where an offense occurs.
Connected by way of their source,
rooted in causes and conditions,
and distinguished by their origin and phrasing.
"Dispute is a legal issue" refers here to a legal issue concerning schism.
